title: Convert a Foreign Licence to a Vietnamese Motorbike Licence
meta_description: How residents convert a foreign licence into a Vietnamese one under Circular 12/2025: who qualifies, which motorbike class you get and where to apply.
h1: Converting a Foreign Licence to a Vietnamese Motorbike Licence
body_markdown:
If you are living in Vietnam rather than passing through, an international driving permit is not the long-term answer. Vietnamese rules expect residents who hold a licence from another country to convert it into a Vietnamese one, and the motorbike class you end up with depends entirely on what your home licence already covers. This guide walks through who can convert, what to prepare, where to apply and what usually goes wrong. It is written for people who will be renting or buying a motorbike over months, not days; if you are collecting a rental this week, the [Hanoi motorbike rental checklist](/en/checklist/) is the more practical starting point.

## Who can convert a foreign licence

The current rules are in Circular 12/2025/TT-BCA, issued by the Ministry of Public Security on 28 February 2025 after responsibility for driving licences moved to the police. According to a [summary of the circular](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/chinh-sach-phap-luat-moi/vn/iThong/80345/quy-dinh-ve-doi-giay-phep-lai-xe-nuoc-ngoai-nam-2025), Article 18(7) says that foreigners who hold a national licence and want to drive in Vietnam must convert it into the corresponding Vietnamese class, unless an international treaty Vietnam has joined says otherwise.

[Article 24(1)](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/chinh-sach-phap-luat-moi/vn/iThong/80345/quy-dinh-ve-doi-giay-phep-lai-xe-nuoc-ngoai-nam-2025) then sets the eligibility conditions. A foreigner who lives, works or studies in Vietnam can apply if they have:

- a national driving licence that is still valid; and
- one of the following, valid for at least three months: a diplomatic or official identity card, a temporary residence card, or a permanent residence card.

The same article lists what cannot be converted: temporary licences, international driving permits, foreign licences that have expired, licences that are damaged, altered or too worn to read, licences with identity discrepancies, and licences not issued by a competent authority. The international permit point is worth underlining. You convert the national card issued by your home country, not the IDP booklet.

The residence requirement is what rules out short-stay visitors. Australia's [Smartraveller](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/asia/vietnam) puts it in plain terms for its citizens: converting an Australian licence requires a valid Vietnamese residence permit of at least three months. Spain's foreign ministry likewise notes that [Spanish residents in Vietnam can exchange their licence](https://www.exteriores.gob.es/es/ServiciosAlCiudadano/Paginas/Detalle-recomendaciones-de-viaje.aspx?trc=Vietnam) and drive legally, while Spanish tourists cannot use their international permit.

## Which motorbike class you will receive

Conversion gives you the Vietnamese class that corresponds to what your licence already allows. It does not add new categories. Under Article 57 of Law 36/2024/QH15 ([consolidated text](https://datafiles.chinhphu.vn/cpp/files/vbpq/2026/3/55-vbhn-vpqh.pdf)), class A1 covers two-wheel motorcycles up to 125 cm³ or with an electric motor up to 11 kW, and class A covers larger motorcycles as well as everything in A1. Car classes start at B.

The practical consequence is spelled out in the [Embassy of Japan's guidance](https://www.vn.emb-japan.go.jp/itpr_ja/Jp_Ryouji_Untenmenkyo.html) for its nationals. If you convert a licence that only covers ordinary cars, the Vietnamese licence you receive also covers only cars, and you cannot ride a motorbike with it. To ride, you either need a home licence that includes motorcycles, or you must convert your car licence and then pass the Vietnamese motorbike theory and riding tests separately. The same embassy page notes that a Japanese automatic-only car licence cannot be converted to a Vietnamese car licence at all.

Before you start, look at the categories printed on your home licence. If you see a motorcycle category such as A or A1 in a European-style licence, or the equivalent motorcycle class in your country's system, you have something to convert. If you only see car categories, conversion alone will not let you ride a scooter in Hanoi.

## Documents to prepare

Article 24(2) of the circular lists the application file. The [Dong Nai police traffic department](https://congan.dongnai.gov.vn/pages/newsdetail.aspx?NewsId=20684&CatId=114) gives the same list in its guidance for applicants:

- the application form for foreigners, using the template annexed to Circular 12/2025;
- a Vietnamese translation of your foreign licence, certified by a notary office in Vietnam or by the Vietnamese diplomatic mission where the translator works, sealed across the attached copy of the licence;
- a driver's health certificate from a qualified medical facility, still valid (the circular exempts foreigners converting for the period stated on their entry visa or temporary residence card);
- a certified paper or electronic copy of your diplomatic or official identity card, temporary residence card or permanent residence card valid for at least three months.

When you submit the file you must show the originals of these documents, and your photo is taken at the counter rather than supplied by you. Bring your passport as well. The Embassy of Japan's list for its nationals includes the passport, and it is the document officials use to match your identity across the other papers.

The translation is where most delays start. It must be a certified translation of the licence itself, not an informal one, and the seal must join the translation to the copy of the licence. Ask the notary office to do both at once.

## Where to apply, how long it takes and the fee

Under [Article 24(3)](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/chinh-sach-phap-luat-moi/vn/iThong/80345/quy-dinh-ve-doi-giay-phep-lai-xe-nuoc-ngoai-nam-2025), you file in person at the provincial police traffic department (Phòng Cảnh sát giao thông) or at a commune-level police office that has been set up as a reception point. Officials check the file, enter it electronically and give you an appointment slip; if they refuse, they must explain why in writing.

The circular then sets the timing. Within one working day of receiving a complete file, the provincial office sends the data to the national Traffic Police Department. The new licence is integrated into the electronic identification system and the holder's electronic ID account within three working days, and the provincial office prints and returns the card within five working days. You can collect it where you applied or ask for it to be posted. The Embassy of Japan's page, updated in July 2026, describes the process for Hanoi applicants as taking up to seven working days after the file is accepted, so plan for some margin.

For Hanoi, the [Embassy of Japan](https://www.vn.emb-japan.go.jp/itpr_ja/Jp_Ryouji_Untenmenkyo.html) names the Ministry of Public Security's Traffic Police Department licensing team at No. 2 Phùng Hưng, Hà Đông, open on weekday mornings and afternoons and on Saturday mornings, with a queue ticket system. Reception arrangements change, so check with the office before you go.

The fee for converting a licence is 135,000 VND per issuance, according to the [Dong Nai police traffic department](https://congan.dongnai.gov.vn/pages/newsdetail.aspx?NewsId=20684&CatId=114); the Embassy of Japan page gives the same figure as of July 2026. Translation, notarisation and the medical check are paid separately to the providers you use.

## How long the converted licence lasts

A Vietnamese motorbike licence issued directly in class A1 or A has no expiry date for Vietnamese holders, but a converted licence for a foreigner is tied to your circumstances. The Embassy of Japan states that the licence it describes is valid until your Vietnamese residence permit expires or your Japanese licence expires, whichever comes first. Check the expiry printed on your own card when you collect it, and put a reminder in your calendar to deal with renewal at the same time as your residence card.

Remember that the home licence still matters after conversion. If it expires and you later need to convert again, you will be asked for a valid foreign licence. Keep it renewed even if you do not plan to drive at home.

## When conversion is not possible

Some people cannot convert, either because they do not hold a residence card for three months or more, or because their licence covers only cars. In that case the options are limited:

- Take the Vietnamese tests. The U.S. Department of State tells its citizens that [to get a Vietnamese driver's licence they should contact the Traffic Police Office of the Provincial Public Security](https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/international-travel/International-Travel-Country-Information-Pages/Vietnam.html) and that a medical exam may be needed.
- Use an international permit if you are only visiting and your country issues the 1968 Vienna Convention model, or if a bilateral agreement covers you. That route has its own rules and is not a substitute for conversion once you live here.
- Do not ride. Ride-hailing, taxis and tours with a driver cover most of what a resident needs while the paperwork is pending.

Riding without the right licence is not a technicality. The [U.S. State Department](https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/international-travel/International-Travel-Country-Information-Pages/Vietnam.html) warns that driving without a Vietnamese licence can lead to fines, arrest or jail, and [Smartraveller](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/asia/vietnam) says travel insurers are likely to reject claims from unlicensed riders.

## A realistic timeline

1. Confirm that your residence card is valid for at least three more months and that your home licence covers motorcycles.
2. Get a certified Vietnamese translation of the licence, sealed to a copy.
3. Book the health check if the exemption does not apply to you.
4. Prepare a certified copy of your residence card.
5. Submit the file in person, have your photo taken and pay the fee.
6. Collect the card or wait for it by post, then check the class and expiry date.

Once the licence is in your hand, the same checks apply to every rental: ask for the registration and insurance papers and record the bike's condition. For general information about renting in Hanoi, return to the [English guide home page](/en/).
